prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, achieving unprecedented accuracy and stability in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I move my preferred configuration from my own first-ranked IceCube candidate (B033) to the optical lattice clock (B041). It has the cleanest combination of the three tests the committee keeps returning to. The discovery is unambiguous: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trade-off between trapping atoms and perturbing the clock transition, and Ye's group pushed fractional uncertainty and stability to the 1e-18 level, beyond the caesium standard and the best ion clocks. It has been independently reproduced and surpassed in many laboratories and is in routine international comparison campaigns. Its reach is broad and concrete: a prospective redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, and tests of fundamental constants and of dark-matter and variation-of-constants models. The attribution is the least contested on the table, a two-person prize in which the originator of the concept and the leader of the performance record are both credited, and all six members who ranked it (Kroll, Lindroth, myself, Olsson, Danielsson and Johansson, all within their top five and with two first places) propose the same two names. As an instrument builder I also value that this is a precision-measurement advance that made a measurable difference to what can be tested, not only a demonstration.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B041 is, in part, a refinement of an already honoured line of work. The 2005 prize recognised the optical frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize recognised control of single trapped ions for clocks, so a committee could judge that the clock record is a very good engineering extension of recognised ground. Its most visible payoff, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened, so recognition rests on demonstrated performance rather than adoption. It was also left unranked by Eriksson and Mehlig and placed only fifth by Danielsson, and its first places come from only two members, whereas B046 has five top-three rankings. Finally, the supplied credit omits other strontium, ytterbium and aluminium-ion clock groups whose work is part of how the field reached its present performance.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B041 first, arguing that the magic-wavelength concept, the control of blackbody and light-shift systematics and the clear distinction from the 2005 frequency-comb prize make it controlled atomic physics with lasting consequences for the SI second.
responses.response: I agree with the physics and the separation from the 2005 prize, and this is the main reason I moved toward B041. I would press one qualification: the 2012 ion-control prize covers part of the same motivation (better clocks), so the citation should be explicit that the recognised achievement is the neutral-atom lattice scheme and its 1e-18 performance, not clocks in general. I also remain unsure how heavily the committee should weigh the credit of the Ytterbium and Al+ groups that you list; I think the two proposed names are defensible, but I accept that a careful reading of the history could add pressure.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B046 first and B033 second, describing twisted bilayer graphene as a theoretical insight confirmed by a decisive measurement, and IceCube as a clear discovery of nature rather than an interpretation, while noting that the IceCube allocation is complicated by the collaboration size and the earlier AMANDA work.
responses.response: I share your view that B033 is a discovery of nature, and I opened with it for that reason, but your attribution point about a collaboration of hundreds and about AMANDA is exactly why I no longer put it first. Halzen and Karle are a credible two-person split in my understanding, yet I cannot verify it from the supplied record, and only the two of us ranked it, so as Chair I should not treat my first place as evidence of committee support. On B046 I agree with your science case but not the maturity reading: my reservation is that the superconducting pairing is unsettled and that Cao and other experimentalists sit outside the credited three.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B046 first and called it clean, because Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive prediction and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experimental discovery, with reproduction by many groups after eight years.
responses.response: B046 is the strongest rival to my preferred configuration and I have kept it as first alternative. I respect the clean theory-plus-experiment pairing, and I agree it has the widest support, with five top-three rankings. Where I differ is on readiness: the question of what the superconductivity is remains open, the first author of the key experimental papers is not credited, and eight years is short compared with a clock programme that has been confirmed and out-performed in many laboratories for over a decade. If the committee judges those points to be minor, I would not resist B046.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first, defended the three-person split of Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf, disclosed that this is his own subfield with Chalmers close to it, and flagged that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes the timing delicate.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure and I think circuit QED is a mature, widely deployed invention. My difficulty is the one you raise yourself: the committee would have to explain why a prize in the same community so soon after 2025 is a distinct discovery. I also note the disputed proposal-versus-experiment emphasis and the omission of Girvin, which makes B031 less clean than B041. I therefore keep it out of my preferred configuration and out of my alternatives, although I ranked it third on opening.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as a sufficiently distinct step beyond the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether the credit for strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks beyond Katori and Ye (for example other groups reaching 1e-18) should alter the two-name configuration.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second, or to recognise the demonstrated performance now.
Whether the maturity concerns on B046 (superconducting pairing, uncredited first authors) are small enough that its broader support should prevail over B041.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B041 from the provided profile. For disclosure: B033 (IceCube) is in my own field of astroparticle physics, and my documented work on Fermi-LAT and PAMELA means I know that community and its multi-messenger programme; I do not claim a personal tie, but I would be willing to recuse from the decision on B033, and I note that I have lowered it in this round for that reason as well as for attribution.
